\chapter{Ayudar — the Same Word as Aid}
\label{ch:spanish-ayudar}
\hlchaptermodality{152}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I help, and hear English aid inside the Spanish word.}

adiutare straight through to aid, and the -di- that also gave hodie -> hoy.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ayudar]{ayudar — \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{}, and it is English \textquotedblleft{}aid\textquotedblright{} in disguise}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-ayudar}



\begin{quote}
You can ask a question now. The next thing to ask for is a hand — and this verb is one you already own in English without knowing it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — a clean, open \emph{a}: \emph{a-yoo-DAR}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one tap at the end, not an English \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ayudar} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to help}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{adiūtāre}, the repeating form of \textbf{adiuvāre}: \textbf{ad-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{iuvāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to help, to delight\textquotedblright{}). To help was to move toward someone.

English borrowed that identical verb through Old French \emph{aidier} and calls it \textbf{aid}. So \emph{ayudar} and \emph{aid} are not merely cousins — they are the \textbf{same word} by two different roads. The family came with it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{aide}, and \textbf{aide-de-camp}, an officer who helps.
  \item \textbf{adjutant} — the officer whose whole job is assisting.
  \item \textbf{adjuvant} — a substance that helps another drug work.
  \item \textbf{coadjutor} — one who helps alongside.
\end{itemize}

The shape change is a rule, not an accident. Latin \textbf{-di-} before a vowel turned into Spanish \textbf{y}: \emph{adiūtāre} $\to$ \textbf{ayudar}, \emph{hodiē} $\to$ \textbf{hoy} (\textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}), \emph{podium} $\to$ \emph{poyo}. Once you have that, the word stops looking arbitrary.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a plain -ar verb, and how to ask for a hand}]
Nothing breaks; the endings are the ones you started with:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{form} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{ayudo} & I help \\
tú & \textbf{ayudas} & you help \\
nosotros & \textbf{ayudamos} & we help \\
ellos/ustedes & \textbf{ayudan} & they help \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Its noun is \textbf{la ayuda} (fem.), \textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{} — the word on relief packages worldwide. Two sentences worth owning: \emph{\textbf{¿Me ayudas?}} (\textquotedblleft{}will you help me?\textquotedblright{} — Spanish uses the plain present where English needs \emph{will}) and, politely, \emph{\textbf{¿Puedo ayudarle?}}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ayudo, ayudas, ayudamos, ayudan\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Me ayudas?\textquotedblright{} — will you help me?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te pregunto\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Me ayudas\textquotedblright{} — I ask you, you help me
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ayudar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}aid, adjutant, adjuvant\textquotedblright{} — one word, two roads
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin pieces build \emph{adiuvāre}? (\textbf{Ad-} \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{iuvāre} \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{}.) What everyday English word is \emph{ayudar}, arriving by French? (\textbf{Aid}.) What sound-law turned \emph{adiūtāre} into \emph{ayudar}, and which other word shows it? (Latin \textbf{-di-} became Spanish \textbf{y}; \emph{hodiē} $\to$ \emph{hoy}.) Next: \textbf{gustar}, the verb that runs backwards.
\end{tcolorbox}
